Repeat hydrographic sections, Argo float profiles and moored sensors agreed on the magnitude and the vertical structure of the anomaly, which left its origin to be settled by freshwater budgets and circulation measurements rather than by salinity records alone. The first line of inquiry was the regional freshwater budget. Over recent decades, at least one of two inputs grew, and perhaps both: Greenland meltwater runoff into the North Atlantic increased, and freshwater export from the Arctic through Fram Strait increased. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report concluded that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation did not collapse during the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, a finding that cannot be squared with a complete shutdown in those same years. The depth reached by convection in that winter is itself evidence that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation continued to operate throughout the period of observed freshening; either the circulation collapsed outright in those decades or it went on working through them, exactly one of the two being the case and both together impossible. What settled the matter, then, was not the salinity anomaly but the transport and convection records that accompanied it."
